ACTUAL RESCUE OPERATION OF PRRC TASK FORCE FLOOD CONTROL

September 12, 2017 - During the landfall of tropical depression Maring, the Task Force Flood Control of the Pasig River Rehabilitation Commission - PRRC was able to rescue six kids who were trapped at a spot along Ermitaño Creek in San Juan City.

"These kids were playing in the rain along the riverbanks of Ermitaño Creek but did not expect that the water level will rise immediately," says Vir Gutierrez Head of PRRC's Abatement and Enforcement Division. "We are glad we saved these children who were so afraid and clinging for their lives," adds Gutierrez. 

The rescue operations were jointly conducted with the Officials of Barangay Ermitaño, and members of the Philippine National Police (PNP).

The Abatement and Enforcement Division is PRRC's latest division under the administration of PRRC Executive Director Jose Antonio "Pepeton" E. Goitia which houses PRRC's River Warriors, River Patrols, and the River Watch. 

#PRRC #PRRCph #TaskForceFloodControl #PusoParaSaIlogPasig

Two Questions:

1. Could the recent fast rising current flood in Tanay and the flooding in Metro Manila have been caused by water release from the dams?
2. What happened to the flood control implemented by President Aquino to end flooding in Metro Manila and what was the cost?

For the flooding in communities around Laguna de Bay, the Philippines should learn from the current flooding in Houston. (True, It is unprecedented and probably will never happen again in a thousand years – a storm that sit over the city for 5 days, that kept drawing moisture from the gulf that dumped 5 feet of rain in Houston.)

Like Houston, which is a swampland, (with population growth and urban sprawl, it became the fourth most populated city in the US) residential development has been allowed even on land which is actually part of Laguna de Bay.

Typhoon Ondoy (Ketsana) is a wake-up call for the Philippines. Fortunately, typhoons blow past the Philippines in only 4 to 6 hours. Only once or twice had tyohoons backtracked.

During typhoon episodes, spill water from Angat dam to Ipo Dam then to Marikina River that joins the Pasig River can inundate the lower portion of Metro Manila. The Mangahan floodway was constructed to direct the water to Laguna de Bay. The problem is, there are now housing developments in what is considered part of the lake. I have been advocating construction of a storm sewer pipe (with bar screens and with tidal gate) at Carlos P. Garcia, downstream of the gated spillway dam (Napindan tidal gates), passing by NAIA with outfall to Manila Bay in Pasay City. This way, flood water can be diverted to Manila Bay during low tide, and the tidal gate closed during high tide, instead of using the Mangahan floodway to send to Laguna de Bay.

Another suggestion is that by a former Civil Engineer professor of FEU (Rafael P Victoria) with extensive work experience in the US, and in the Middle East,. He wrote:
Additional problems I remember about metro-Manila flooding
The esteros clattered with debris and often times clogged by squatters temporary housings; the existence of the combined sewer system that used daily pumping to drain most of the sewers to accommodate incoming runoff; poor maintenance of street gutters and inlets; and tidal rises timed wth extended rainfalls causing pasig river and esteros to fail in delivering storm water to Manila bay. It is sad that up to now Manila floodings remained a major crisis. You have suggested major solutions to the problem. May be if the major clean up of Pasig River and esteros of Manila and Quezon Cities, as well as other cities around them, some major improvements would be attained. Regarding esteros, I suggest to make them all concrete channels and make roads out of their surfaces. That may assist in some measure in reducing the traffic crisis of the cities.

I’ve been staying at my mom’s house in Batangas. The other night, I was having a drink with neighbors on their porch when they commented how things had changed around here. The main road in our village is now flanked with 2-story concrete houses.

We spent most of our childhood within flimsy walls. The house across ours was built from sawali (interwoven bamboo splits). The one beside it used to be made of nipa leaves. Our house was made of sawdust.

SAWDUST.

You know when you mix sawdust with resin and they harden, they become these thin boards? The house I grew up in was a bungalow made of these sawdust boards.

There were parts that were made of plywood, but much of the walls were these boards. It’s amazing how we weren’t really directly hit by strong typhoons growing up. The only thing I clearly remember is Rosing, but it was the flood that we worried about, not the winds.

Our house then had a living area with bamboo furniture, a kitchen where I found SNAKES while cleaning on two separate occasions, and two small bedrooms. Bedroom 1 was where my dad slept. He was sick and he wanted to be alone all the time so he had that room to himself.

Bedroom 2 was where the rest of the family stayed. The room was cozy (sugarcoating!!!). It was as long as the bed. Three of the sides of the bed touched the walls (there were no gaps in between)! One side had little space. My mom, my brother, my sister and I slept on that bed. All four of us! Our feet dangled from one edge because our bodies were longer than the bed.

This is also the reason that even up to now, even when our house is much bigger, with four rooms, one for each of us, WE STILL SLEEP IN THE SAME ROOM. Out of habit. Out of comfort. We grew up that way.

Yep, still in the same room. (Except my brother coz he has his own family now.)

I don’t even know why I’m sharing this. But I’m writing this in the living room of our house and remembered the howling winds that I woke up to this morning. Another typhoon has passed. I’m safe and dry, with a cup of tea in between my palms, a roof above me, and walls that aren’t made of sawdust. And I thought, if this happened 20 years ago, it would be a very different story. 

- Yosh

INUNDATED LAGUNA UNDER STATE OF CALAMITY

MANILA - Officials have declared Laguna province under state of calamity after tropical storm "Maring" and typhoon "Lannie" triggered massive flooding that forced thousands of residents to seek safer ground, Governor Ramil Hernandez said Wednesday. 

The Provincial Council approved the state of calamity in a special session Tuesday, Hernandez said in a phone interview with ABS-CBN News. 

A state of calamity means local officials can tap emergency funds for the evacuees and impose a price freeze on basic commodities. 

Heavy rains have swamped low-lying areas along river banks and the Laguna Lake. Among the worst-hit areas were the towns of San Pedro, Cabuyao, Calamba, and Sta Rosa, Hernandez said. 

Initial cost of damage to property was pegged at P13 million while damage to agriculture was at P6.7 million. 

Some 1,600 families or 6,000 individuals have sought shelter at evacuation centers, the governor added. 

The body of a drowned 15-year-old boy was recovered from Calamba's San Cristobal River while least 6 others remained missing, Hernandez said. 

"Maging alerto po tayo. Kapag po sinabi ng barangay, sinabi ng authorities na kailangan nang lumikas, huwag po tayong magbakasali," Hernandez told his constituents. 

"Iyung nangyari po ngayon, karamihan po ng mga missing, iyun po ang mga hindi nag-evacuate." 

Maring and Lannie are set to leave the Philippine area of responsibility late Wednesday, state weather bureau PAGASA said. 

All storm signals have been lifted, but Maring will still bring light to moderate rains in Palawan, Oriental Mindoro, Zambales, Bataan, and Batangas, PAGASA warned.
